usedTryThisNowFrames: Pick one system you rely on and label it fragile, robust, or antifragile by asking what a small shock would actually do to it.
Name one reserve you have been tempted to cut and write the specific disruption it would help you survive long enough to learn from.
Look at one routine you protect from friction and decide whether it is more like a machine wearing down or an organism losing signal.
Choose one challenge you use for growth and write the smallest sign that it has crossed from training load into damage.
Find one decision being centralized for neatness and write where a small local error would be caught faster.
Pick one decision this week and add one small random trial only after writing the maximum acceptable loss.
Before fixing one irritation, write what warning it might be carrying and what would happen if that warning disappeared.
Take one forecast you are relying on and write the downside if it is wrong before revising the forecast itself.
For one recommendation you heard today, write the bet it implies and whose loss would prove it wrong.
Write one attractive upside you want, then write the exact loss that must be clipped before you pursue it.
Split one plan into what must not fail and what can be risked cheaply for upside.
Find one place where you can buy time, access, or a reversible right without accepting the full obligation.
Take one stuck problem and run the smallest real-world trial before improving the explanation.
Choose one pair you have been treating as equivalent and write how each behaves under one bad shock.
Look at one success story and write what the official explanation may have ignored from the people doing the work.
Add one bounded trial to a decision where planning has stalled, and define the stop condition first.
Take one debate that has become abstract and write the smallest real consequence that would settle part of it.
Find one risk being averaged and ask whether the same total harm arrives as one blow or many small taps.
For one fix you like, write the clearest way it could produce the inverse of its intended result.
Before adopting one new tool or rule, compare it with the older survivor and name the stress each has actually faced.
For one intervention, write the visible benefit, the hidden downside, and whether the payoff is convex or concave.
Remove one clearly harmful input for 24 hours before adding any new improvement.
For one decision you influence, name who gets the upside, who carries the downside, and what would align them.
Pick one professional rule and write the actual harm it is meant to prevent, who suffers it, and who should share it.
Sort three current commitments into protect from volatility, expose to bounded variation, or stop because the downside is exported.
